country.comment: Single-country policy case study examining water law and policy reform in Malawi.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Title and Abstract; PDF pp. 5-13, Section 'Case study: Malawi'

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative/doctrinal-policy case study relying on legal/policy texts and secondary literature; no primary statistical analysis or numeric treatment effect is estimated.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Examining Malawi's 1995 Water Works Act, 1999 Water Resources Policy and Strategy, Article 20 of the Constitution, and 2000 National Gender Policy alongside secondary sources, the study finds that decentralized user-pays water charges, irrigation farmers' association membership fees, and gender-blind policy mainstreaming disproportionately burden Malawian women (who comprise 75% of the poor and head 30% of households), pricing poor women out of safe household and irrigation water, increasing reliance on distant contaminated sources, and leaving Community Water Board leadership predominantly male despite female majority membership.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 8-12, Sections 'The Malawian water law reforms', 'The impacts of the reforms upon women', and 'The incorporation of women in policy'

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling is <=2; coded as 0 because the paper conducts no primary empirical data collection or statistical testing and explicitly notes (PDF p. 9) that much of its impact analysis focuses on intended implementation and predicted impacts inferred from policy texts, feminist/entitlements theory, and secondary reports (with only brief secondary descriptive citations to early CWB composition and water charges).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 9, Section 'The impacts of the reforms upon women'; PDF pp. 10-12

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines user-pays household water tariffs and farmers' association irrigation membership fees (BURDEN: fees); stakeholder participation, male-dominated Community Water Board leadership, and non-binding gender quotas in national policy (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: participation); gendered matrilineal/patrilineal land inheritance, state water custodianship, and productive water withdrawal permits (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, property); and unclear allocation of maintenance/funding responsibilities and ministerial planning capacity across government, NGOs, catchment authorities, and communities (planning, institutional_fragmentation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, fees, participation, tenure, property, planning, institutional_fragmentation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 7-12, Sections 'Gender in Malawi', 'The Malawian water law reforms', 'The impacts of the reforms upon women', and 'The incorporation of women in policy'

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes household and irrigation water access, user-charge affordability, contamination of alternative free water sources (service_quality), national safe-water coverage targets and estimates (47%-72%), and infrastructure breakdown/dry wells (service_reliability, with up to 50% of water points non-functional).

study_design.comment: Desk-based policy and legal-institutional case study applying feminist development theory (WID/WAD/GAD) and Sen/Mehta entitlements theory to Malawian water statutes, national policy documents, and secondary literature, without primary fieldwork or a systematic search protocol.
study_design.value: Qualitative policy and legal-institutional case study based on document analysis and non-systematic secondary literature review
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 3-5, Sections 'The global water debate' and 'Feminist theory'; PDF p. 5, Section 'Case study: Malawi'; PDF pp. 8-12

evidence_quotes.quote: Since the mid-1990s, Malawi has undertaken a process of water policy reform.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 8, Section 'The Malawian water law reforms'
evidence_quotes.quote: The first significant changes in Malawian water law, in terms of implementation, took place in the form of the 1995 Water Works Act, which resulted in the establishment of Community Water Boards, (CWBs). These were to be self-funded by water use fees.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 9, Section 'The impacts of the reforms upon women'
evidence_quotes.quote: Given the short period of time since these policies have begun to be implemented, much of the following discussion focuses on the intended implementation of the reforms and their predicted impacts. It also draws on evidence from other countries that have implemented similar reforms.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 10, Section 'The impacts of the reforms upon women'
evidence_quotes.quote: As the gatherers of water, it is poor women who must walk further to fetch water that is not charged for and this is often contaminated, placing further pressure on their time and energy (Tenthani, 2002).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 10, Section 'The impacts of the reforms upon women'
evidence_quotes.quote: Unfortunately, leadership of the CWBs is almost entirely male and, as such, the decision-making power is outside the control of women (Tenthani, 2002; Mulwafu et al., 2002).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 11, Section 'The incorporation of women in policy'
evidence_quotes.quote: Further to this, the reformed water policies signal the intention to improve water coverage nationally (Republic of Malawi, 2000) but there is no mechanism in place to ensure that gains are gender equitable.
